a: In the thirty-fifth jubilee
p: The book dates every birth and marriage by jubilees of 49 years and weeks of seven years.
b: Jubilees counts time from creation in blocks: a jubilee of 49 years, made of seven "weeks" of seven years each. So "the thirty-fifth jubilee, the third week, its first year" means that 34 jubilees (1,666 years) and two weeks (14 years) have passed: this is year 1681 from creation by the book's own count. Charles 1902 prints the same figure in his margin. Genesis gives ages instead (Genesis 11:20–21). The book's jubilee is 49 years, not the 50 of Leviticus 25:10.

a: Reu married a woman named Ara, the daughter of Ur son of Kesed
p: Genesis 11 lists only fathers and sons; Jubilees gives each man a wife and her father.
b: Genesis 11:20–22 says only that Reu fathered Serug and Serug fathered Nahor. Jubilees names the mothers too, here and through chapters 11 and 12. Charles 1902 notes that a Syriac list of "the wives of the patriarchs" taken from Jubilees, and one Greek manuscript of Genesis, give Reu's wife a similar name, Ora. The names show the book's interest in who married whom, a concern that grows later in the book.

a: the sons of Noah began to fight one another
t: The world goes bad again after the Flood
p: Genesis has the first kingdoms begin with Nimrod; Jubilees tells of war, slavery and idols.
b: Genesis says only that Nimrod "was the first to become a hero on the earth" (Genesis 10:8) and that his kingdom began with Babel (Genesis 10:10). Jubilees paints a whole age: war, captives, eating blood, walled cities, kings, weapons and slave markets. Goes beyond the Bible: no book of the 66 describes this age. Charles 1902 shows that later Christian chroniclers knew this picture: Epiphanius puts the start of idolatry in Serug's time, and Cedrenus says that in Serug's day men set up generals and kings and first made weapons.

a: ate blood
p: Eating blood was the very thing God forbade Noah.
b: "Only, flesh with its life, its blood, you must not eat" (Genesis 9:4). Jubilees has already made this law a heavy matter for Noah's children (see chapter 6 and 7:28–33). Here the first sign of the new corruption is that Noah's descendants shed blood and eat it, the two sins the command joined. Acts 15:20 still asks Gentile believers to keep away from blood.

a: gear for battle
p: The Ge'ez says "gear of the field"; in this list of wars it most likely means weapons.
b: The words are nəwayä ḥäql, literally "gear (or tools) of the field." The list around them is about war: fighting, captives, strong cities, teaching sons to fight. So the Plain English Translation takes it as gear for battle. Charles rendered it "arms." A reader could also hear farm tools, but that fits the verse less well.

a: the city of Ara of the Chaldeans
p: The book turns the place name "Ur Kasdim" into two men, Ur and his father Kesed.
b: Genesis calls Abram's home Ur Kasdim, "Ur of the Chaldeans" (Genesis 11:28). Jubilees explains the name as a city built by a man called Ur, son of Kesed, the ancestor of the Kasdim (Chaldeans). Charles 1902 points this out, and he takes "Ara" to be a slip for Ur. Genesis 22:22 does know a Kesed, a son of Nahor, but he lived later.
orig: ሀገረ አራሃ እንተ ከልዴዎን (hägärä ʾäraha ʾəntä käldewon)

a: They made molten images for themselves
p: From here on, Charles's numbers (and most older books') are one lower than this site's.
b: The site follows the verse numbers of VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989). R. H. Charles, whose 1902 and 1913 translations most older books cite, counted 11:3 and 11:4 here as one verse. So from this verse to the end of the chapter his numbers are one lower: this site's 11:11 (Mastema's ravens) is his 11:10, and Abram's birth, 11:15 here, falls in his 11:13–14.

a: Cruel spirits helped them and led them astray
p: Jubilees says evil spirits stood behind the first idol-makers and urged them on.
b: These are the spirits of 10:1–14, left on earth under Mastema after the Flood. The book's point is that idolatry is not only human foolishness; spirits feed it. Agrees in idea: Deuteronomy 32:17 says Israel sacrificed to demons, not God, and Paul writes that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons (1 Corinthians 10:20). Goes beyond: the Bible never tells the story of how idol worship first began.

a: Prince Mastema
p: Mäkʷännä Mastema, "Prince Mastema": the leader of the evil spirits in Jubilees.
b: In 10:8 Mastema first appears as the chief of the spirits (mälʾäkä mänafsət), and God lets him keep a tenth of them. Here he is "Prince Mastema," and he sends them out to do harm. In this verse VanderKam's Ge'ez spells the name wästema (ወስቴማ), with w where 10:8, 11:11 and 17:16 have m (mästema, መስቴማ); the Plain English Translation gives the usual form, Mastema. The Plain English Translation keeps the name Mastema; the book calls him Satan only at 10:11. He plays the part that the accuser plays in Job 1–2 and that later Jewish and Christian writers give to Satan: Charles 1902, on 17:16, compares a Talmud passage (Sanhedrin 89b) where Satan, not God, prompts Abraham's test.

a: those who had been put under his hand
p: The spirits work only because they were given to Mastema, an idea close to Job 1-2.
b: "Put under his hand" (täwhəbu taḥtä ʾədehu) is passive: someone gave them to him. In 10:8–9 God grants Mastema a tenth of the spirits. Agrees in idea: in Job the accuser can touch Job only as far as God allows (Job 1:12; Job 2:6). Goes beyond: Jubilees makes this a standing arrangement for the whole human race, with a named prince and a fixed share.

a: That is why Serug was given the name Serug
p: The book explains Serug's name from the people's "turning aside" to sin.
b: The Ge'ez says everyone "turned" (tämäyṭä) to sin. Charles 1902 thinks the Hebrew behind it played on the name Serug (S-R-G) and the verb sur, "turn aside." Jubilees often explains names this way (see Terah in 11:12). In the text Charles used, the boy is first called Seroh (11:1) and renamed Serug here; in VanderKam's text he is Serug both times (see the variant at 11:1).
orig: ተጸውዐ ስሙ ለሴሩክ ሴሩክ (täṣäwʿä səmu läseruk seruk)

a: a daughter of his father's brother
p: Serug marries his cousin; Terah too marries a cousin (11:14), and Abram a half-sister (12:9).
b: Jubilees records several marriages inside the family in this line: Serug's cousin Melka, Terah's cousin Edna (11:14), and Abram's half-sister Sarai (12:9). Genesis shows the same wish to marry within the clan when Abraham sends for a wife for Isaac "to my own land and my own relatives" (Genesis 24:4). The book will press this point hard later, against marrying outsiders.

a: and he worshiped idols
p: Joshua 24:2 says Terah and the fathers "served other gods"; Jubilees names Serug as one of them.
b: Joshua 24:2 says of the time before Abraham: "Terah, the father of Abraham and Nahor, lived there, and they served other gods." Agrees: Jubilees fills in that statement, starting the idol worship two generations earlier with Serug, and having Nahor learn the omens of the Chaldeans (11:8). Abram will be the one who breaks with it (11:16; 12:1–14).

a: how to tell the future and read omens by the signs in the sky
p: Nahor learns the star-lore of the Chaldeans, the very arts the law of Moses forbids.
b: The Chaldeans were famous for star-reading; in Daniel they are a class of learned men called in with "the magicians, the enchanters, the sorcerers" (Daniel 2:2). Deuteronomy 18:10 forbids anyone who "practices divination, reads signs, looks for omens." Jubilees sets this learning in Abram's own family so that his turning away from it (12:16–18) stands out. Charles 1902 shows the Byzantine writer Cedrenus repeating that Nahor's father taught him omens and Chaldean divination.
orig: ለተማርዮ ወለተሰግሎ በተአምረ ሰማይ (lätämaryo wälätäsäglo bätäʾämrä sämay)

a: lived in Ur of the Chaldeans
p: The Ge'ez names Ur twice here; the Plain English Translation names it once.
b: The Ge'ez says, word for word, "he lived in Ur, in (the city) of those of Ur of the Chaldeans" (wəstä ʾur wəstä zäʾlä ʾur kälädawiyan). Charles has simply "in Ur of the Chaldees." The Plain English Translation gives the place once, as in 11:7 and Genesis 11:28.
orig: ውስተ ኡር ውስተ ዘእለ ኡር ከለዳዊያን (wəstä ʾur wəstä zäʾlä ʾur kälädawiyan)

a: Iyaska, the daughter of Nestag
p: In Genesis 11:29 Iscah is Haran's daughter; here she is Nahor the elder's wife.
b: Genesis 11:29 names "Milcah and Iscah" as daughters of Haran. Jubilees uses both names for an earlier generation: Melka is Serug's wife (11:7) and Iyaska is the wife of Nahor, Terah's father. Charles 1902 notes that the Syriac list of the patriarchs' wives has the same name for Nestag. Genesis 11:24 gives Nahor's son Terah with no mother named.

a: Prince Mastema sent ravens and other birds
p: Jerome cites this legend from an apocryphal Genesis to explain Terah's name.
b: Charles 1902 found three later writers who knew this story. Jerome, in his Letter 78 to Fabiola (on Numbers 33:27), says that in an apocryphal book of Genesis, Abraham's father got his name, "one who drives away," by driving off the ravens that were ruining people's grain. A Syriac retelling under Ephrem's name and the historian Bar Hebraeus tell how young Abram drove the ravens away by calling on God. So Jerome, writing around AD 400, knew this story and where it came from.

a: That is why he named him Terah
p: The verse ties Terah's name to the ravens that made people poor.
b: The Ge'ez verb is yastäṣensəwomu, "they made them poor." Charles 1902 suggests the Hebrew had a verb close to the name Terah, and that the Ge'ez reflects a Greek word for "beggared" or "oppressed." Jerome understood the name the other way round, as "driver away" (see 11:11). Either way the book makes a name tell a story, as Genesis often does.

a: Edna, the daughter of Abram
p: George Syncellus cites "the Little Genesis" for this: Abraham's mother's father was called Abram.
b: George Syncellus writes in his Chronography that "the Little Genesis" says Abraham's grandfather on his mother's side was called Abram (as quoted in Charles 1902). That matches this verse and 11:15. Charles also notes that later Jewish writings name Terah's wife differently, as Amthelai, daughter of Karnebo (Babylonian Talmud Baba Bathra 91a). Genesis never names Abram's mother.

a: He named him Abram
p: Genesis 11:26 says only that Terah, at seventy, fathered Abram, Nahor and Haran.
b: "Terah lived 70 years and fathered Abram, Nahor and Haran" (Genesis 11:26). Jubilees gives a date instead: by its count this is year 1876 from creation. It also makes Abram the eldest who is named; Haran and Nahor appear only as his brothers in 12:8–11.

a: When he was two weeks of years old
t: How old was Abram when he found God?
p: Jubilees says fourteen. Jewish teachers gave other ages: three, or forty-eight.
b: Two weeks of years are fourteen years (see 11:18). Syncellus, drawing on this book, says that in his fourteenth year Abraham recognized the God of all (as quoted in Charles 1902). Charles also lists rabbinic answers: Simeon ben Lakish said Abraham knew God at three years old (Genesis Rabbah 30), and Rabbi Hanina said in his forty-eighth year. The question shows how much Jews of every age wanted to know what Genesis 12:1 leaves out: why God called this man.

a: He began to pray to the Creator of all things
p: Genesis begins with God's call. Jubilees first shows a boy who rejects idols and prays.
b: In Genesis Abram's story starts with God's words, "Go on your way" (Genesis 12:1), with no reason given. Goes beyond the Bible: Jubilees gives him a conversion first. Christian readers have noted that this shifts the weight: in Genesis God's choice comes first and Abram's trust follows (Genesis 15:6; Nehemiah 9:7). In Jubilees the young Abram seeks God, and God answers his prayer (12:22).

a: "Do not come down! Go back to the place you came from!"
t: The boy who turns back the ravens
p: Abram's first deed in the book is to undo Mastema's harm to the harvest.
b: Mastema sent the birds to ruin the land (11:11); the boy Abram sends them back. The later Syriac retelling quoted in Charles 1902 adds that Abram called on God, and God answered "Here I am" and sent the ravens off. Goes beyond: Genesis has no story of Abram's boyhood. But the picture fits Genesis's promise that through Abram blessing would come to the clans of the earth (Genesis 12:3): here the first to be blessed are the Chaldean farmers.

a: seventy times
p: The Ge'ez says simply "he did (so) seventy times"; Charles adjusted the verb.
b: VanderKam's text reads wägäbrä ... säbʿa, "he did this ... seventy" (times). Charles 1902 suggested changing the verb to "he caused to turn back." The Plain English Translation keeps the text, which makes good sense as it stands. Seventy is a number of fullness in Jubilees and the Bible (Genesis 46:27; Matthew 18:22).

a: They built a box above the ground, facing the frame of the plow
p: Claude's theory: the seed box is the book's answer to Mastema, wisdom that guards bread.
b: This is Claude's reading, not a claim of the book. Mastema's attack on Ur was an attack on food (11:11–13). Abram meets it twice: first by prayer and command (11:19–21), then by a tool that buries the seed as the plow cuts the furrow, so the birds never see it. The book likes to make the fathers founders of useful skills: Enoch learns writing (4:17) and Noah receives a book of healing (10:12–13). Here the friend of God is also the man who feeds his neighbors, which fits Proverbs' picture of wisdom as a builder and provider (Proverbs 3:19–20; Proverbs 9:1–5).

a: What help or joy do we get from these idols
p: Abram's speech borrows the prophets' mockery of idols.
b: Samuel warned Israel not to turn aside after "hollow things, which cannot help you or rescue you" (1 Samuel 12:21). Abram's speech (12:2–5) gathers many such lines from the prophets and Psalms, and puts them in the mouth of Israel's first father. Charles 1902 notes that the Byzantine lexicon Suda knew a tradition of Abraham at fourteen telling his father, "There is no other God except the one in the heavens, who also created the whole world."

a: There is no spirit in them at all
p: The Psalms and the prophets say the same of idols: there is no breath in them.
b: Jeremiah says of the idol-maker's image, "there is no breath in them" (Jeremiah 10:14), and Habakkuk, "there is no breath inside it at all" (Habakkuk 2:19). Psalm 135:17 says, "not even breath is in their mouths." The Ge'ez mänfäs means both spirit and breath. Abram's argument is that a thing with no spirit cannot give life, while God is the source of "all life" (12:4).

a: who sends down rain and dew on the earth
p: Jeremiah asks whether any idol can make it rain. Abram answers before Jeremiah asks.
b: "Can any of the nations' empty idols make it rain?" (Jeremiah 14:22). Rain is the test Abram puts first, and it will matter again when he watches the stars for signs of rain (12:16–18). Jesus says the Father "sends rain" on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45), and Paul tells the people of Lystra that God gave them rain from heaven (Acts 14:17).

a: you carry them on your shoulders
t: Gods that have to be carried
p: Isaiah's picture of idol bearers: "They hoist it on their shoulders and haul it."
b: Isaiah mocks the gods of Babylon: "They hoist it on their shoulders and haul it" (Isaiah 46:7), while the LORD carries his people (Isaiah 46:3–4). Jeremiah says the same: "Someone always has to pick them up, for they take no steps" (Jeremiah 10:5). Abram's speech is a short sermon against idols, shaped from the prophets' own words.

a: what can I do about the people who have made me serve in front of them?
p: Jubilees makes Terah a man who knows the truth but fears the crowd. Others made him an idol-maker.
b: Jubilees is gentle with Terah: he knows idols are nothing, but he serves them because the people would kill him (12:7). Later, Terah blesses Abram's journey in God's name (12:29). Other traditions are harsher. Epiphanius, quoted in Charles 1902, says image-making began with Terah's craft as a potter. Joshua 24:2 says only that Terah "served other gods."

a: his father's daughter
p: Jubilees follows Genesis 20:12. Leviticus 18:9 later forbids such a marriage.
b: In Genesis Abraham says of Sarah, "she is in fact my sister, my father's daughter though not my mother's, and she became my wife" (Genesis 20:12). Jubilees takes that at face value. The law of Moses later forbids it (Leviticus 18:9; Leviticus 20:17). Charles 1902 notes that rabbinic tradition held such a marriage lawful for Noah's descendants before Sinai. Jubilees, which usually shows the fathers already keeping Moses' laws, lets this one stand.

a: a woman named Sarai
p: The Ge'ez calls her Sora until God renames her in 15:15.
b: VanderKam's Ge'ez calls her Sora here and up to 15:15, where she becomes Sara. Charles 1902 notes that the Ethiopic Bible's Genesis 17:15 has the same forms. The Plain English Translation uses the usual English names, Sarai and then Sarah, as Genesis does (Genesis 17:15).

a: burned the house of idols
p: Jubilees has Abram burn the idols. Later legend had Abram himself thrown into the fire.
b: Charles 1902 traces a later Jewish legend: the tyrant Nimrod threw Abram into a furnace for refusing to worship, and God saved him. It grew from reading Ur in "Ur of the Chaldeans" as Hebrew ur, "fire," and from Genesis 15:7, "I am the LORD, who brought you out from Ur." It is found in the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 11:28 and in Genesis Rabbah 38, and Jerome reports it in his Hebrew Questions on Genesis. Jubilees knows nothing of Abram in the furnace. Here it is Haran who dies in the fire, which may be the seed of the later story. The Byzantine writers Syncellus and Cedrenus retell this verse.

a: died in Ur of the Chaldeans before his father Terah
p: Genesis 11:28 says only that Haran died before his father. Jubilees says how.
b: "Haran died while his father Terah was still alive, in the land where he was born, in Ur of the Chaldeans" (Genesis 11:28). The Hebrew ʿal-pene means "in the face of": before his father, either in time or in his sight. Jubilees reads it both ways: he died in the fire, in front of Terah. Jerome, quoted in Charles 1902, reports that the Jews of his day said Haran was "consumed by fire" because he would not worship it.
orig: עַל־פְּנֵי תֶּרַח אָבִיו (ʿal-pene Teraḥ ʾaviv), "in the face of Terah his father" (Genesis 11:28)

a: to go to the land of Lebanon and the land of Canaan
p: Genesis 11:31 has Terah set out for Canaan and stop at Haran. Jubilees adds Lebanon.
b: "They went out with them from Ur of the Chaldeans to go to the land of Canaan. They came as far as Haran and settled there" (Genesis 11:31). Jubilees adds Lebanon, perhaps thinking of the northern road. In this book Terah leads the move, but Abram has already broken with the idols; in Acts 7:2 God appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia before Haran.

a: In the sixth week, in its fifth year
p: By the book's own count Abram is now 75, the age Genesis gives when he leaves Haran.
b: Abram was born in year 1876 from creation (11:15). The fifth year of the sixth week of the fortieth jubilee is year 1951. So Abram is 75, exactly the age of Genesis 12:4: "Abram was seventy-five years old when he left Haran." Jubilees places the night of star-watching, the prayer and God's call (12:16–24) in that year. Charles 1902 gives the same figures.

a: He watched the stars from evening until morning to see what the year would bring in rain
t: Reading the year from the stars
p: On the first day of the seventh month Abram tries to foretell the rains of the coming half-year.
b: The first day of the seventh month begins the rainy half of the year in the land. Charles 1902 explains that Abram is trying to learn from the stars what the six rainy months would bring. This is the Chaldeans' craft he was raised in (11:8). The Byzantine writer Cedrenus, who had this book before him, says Abram had been well trained in that science (as quoted in Charles 1902).

a: All the signs of the stars and the signs of the moon and the sun are in the Lord's hand
t: The stars serve God; they do not rule
p: Abram stops searching the stars because God, not the stars, decides the rain.
b: Agrees with the Bible: Genesis makes the lights "signs" set by God (Genesis 1:14), and Jeremiah says, "Do not panic at the signs in the sky, / though the nations panic at them" (Jeremiah 10:2). Deuteronomy 4:19 warns Israel not to serve the sun, moon and stars. Charles 1902 notes that the rabbis tell a similar story: God told Abram he was a prophet, not a star-gazer (Genesis Rabbah 44). Abram's question, "Why am I searching them out?", is the moment he leaves the Chaldeans' wisdom behind.

a: God Most High
p: ʾAmlak ləʿul, "God Most High," the title Melchizedek uses in Genesis 14.
b: Abram's first prayer uses the title ʾamlak ləʿul, "God Most High," which in Genesis appears first on Melchizedek's lips (Genesis 14:18–20) and then in Abram's oath (Genesis 14:22). The Plain English Translation renders ləʿul "the Most High" throughout, as in 1 Enoch. Jubilees uses the title often for the God of the fathers (13:16; 13:29; 16:27).

a: You and your kingdom I have chosen
p: The text ends the prayer's first part with Abram's choice; Charles moved the line.
b: VanderKam's text, like the manuscripts Charles used, puts "you and your kingdom I have chosen" at the end of the verse, and the Plain English Translation keeps that order. Charles 1902 moved the line forward, after "you alone are my God." The word mäläkot means kingdom or lordship. In Genesis God chooses Abram (Nehemiah 9:7); here Abram also chooses God, as Israel is called to choose in Joshua 24:15.

a: Save me from the power of the evil spirits who rule over the thoughts of the human heart
p: Abram asks to be kept from the spirits that rule human thoughts, as Jesus taught "rescue us from the evil one."
b: Agrees in idea: the Lord's Prayer ends, "rescue us from the evil one" (Matthew 6:13), and Paul speaks of "the spirit who is now active among those who refuse to obey" (Ephesians 2:2). Goes beyond Genesis: Abram prays no such prayer there. Jubilees puts it in his mouth because the book has just shown Mastema's spirits misleading the nations (11:4–5). Noah prays a similar prayer in 10:3–6.

a: the word of the Lord was sent to him through me
p: The narrator, the angel of the presence, says he carried God's call to Abram.
b: In Genesis 12:1 "The LORD said to Abram." In Jubilees the angel who tells Moses this whole story (1:27) says the word came "through me," literally "by my hand." The book makes angels the go-betweens of God's word, the same idea the New Testament uses for the law at Sinai: it was "arranged through angels, by the hand of a mediator" (Galatians 3:19; Acts 7:53; Hebrews 2:2).

a: Go out from your land, from your kin and from your father's house
p: Genesis 12:1–3, nearly word for word. Stephen's quotation in Acts leaves out "your father's house."
b: Jubilees follows Genesis 12:1–3 closely here. Charles 1902 notes that Stephen's quotation in Acts 7:3 drops "from your father's house": "Go out of your land and away from your kin, and come on to whatever land I show you." In Jubilees the phrase matters, because Abram must leave Terah in Haran for a time (12:28–31).

a: All the nations of the earth will find blessing in you
p: The Ge'ez says "all the nations of the earth," the wording Paul quotes in Galatians 3:8.
b: Genesis 12:3 in Hebrew has mishpeḥot, "clans" (the site: "All the clans of the earth will find blessing in you"). The Ge'ez has ʾäḥzabä mədr, "the nations of the earth," like the promise in Genesis 18:18 and Genesis 22:18. Paul quotes the promise in that form: "All the nations will be blessed in you" (Galatians 3:8). Jubilees, which keeps Israel apart from the nations, still keeps the promise of blessing for them.

a: I will be God to you, to your son, to your son's son and to all your offspring
p: Jubilees adds to the first call the promise Genesis gives later, "I will be God to you."
b: "I will be God to you and to your offspring after you" belongs in Genesis to the covenant of circumcision (Genesis 17:7). Jubilees already speaks it at the call, and "to your son and your son's son" looks ahead to the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Exodus 3:6). Goes beyond: the wording is new, but the idea is the Bible's.

a: in the language that has been revealed
p: Jubilees says Hebrew was lost to everyone at Babel and given back to Abram. Others said Eber kept it.
b: "The overthrow" is the fall of the tower in 10:26, where the Ge'ez uses the same word (dəqät). Jubilees says that from then no one spoke Hebrew until the angel opened Abram's mouth. Charles 1902 shows that this view passed into the Christian Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions (1.30), which speaks of "the Hebrew language, given by God to the human race." Another view held that Eber alone kept the old language because he did not help build the tower: Charles cites Diodorus of Antioch, Augustine (City of God 16.11) and Cedrenus for it.

a: in Hebrew, in the language of creation
p: The angel taught Abram Hebrew, the tongue God used at creation. Syncellus quotes this line.
b: The Ge'ez is ʿəbraysəṭ bälsanä fəṭrät. The claim is that Hebrew was the language in which God made the world ("God said," Genesis 1:3). George Syncellus quotes it from "the Little Genesis": the angel speaking to Moses said, "I taught Abraham the Hebrew language, as from the beginning of creation" (Greek in Charles 1902).
orig: ዕብራይስጥ በልሳነ ፍጥረት (ʿəbraysəṭ bälsanä fəṭrät); Greek in Syncellus: τὴν Ἑβραΐδα γλῶσσαν κατὰ τὴν ἀπ' ἀρχῆς κτίσεως

a: He took the books of his fathers
p: Jubilees imagines a written chain of teaching from Enoch through Noah to Abram and beyond.
b: Enoch was the first to write (4:17), Noah wrote down what the angels taught him (10:13), and now Abram copies "the books of his fathers" and studies them. Later Jacob hands his books to Levi (45:16). Goes beyond the Bible: Genesis never mentions writing among the fathers. The claim gives the book's own teaching a long pedigree, older than Moses but agreeing with him.

a: the six months of the rains
p: The winter half of the year, the time for study.
b: Charles 1902 notes that the phrase matches the Talmud's "days of rain," the winter half of the year, set against "the days of the sun," the summer. Farm work slackened in the rains, so it was the season for study. The night of star-watching that opened this season was the first of the seventh month (12:16).

a: May the eternal God make your path straight
p: The idol-serving father sends his son off with a blessing in the name of the eternal God.
b: Terah blesses in the name of "the eternal God" and "the Lord." Genesis gives Terah no words at all. The wish echoes Proverbs, "he will level your paths" (Proverbs 3:6), and Tobit's blessing on his son's journey, "May God in heaven bring you there safely and bring you back to me in good health" (Tobit 5:17). It also makes Terah, who knew the truth about idols (12:6), end his part in the story well.

a: come and take me to you
t: Did Abram leave his father to die?
p: Jubilees has Abram leave Haran with Terah's blessing, planning to come back for him.
b: In Genesis Terah dies in Haran at 205 (Genesis 11:32), but the dates mean he was still alive when Abram left at 75 (Genesis 11:26; Genesis 12:4). Stephen says Abraham left Haran "After his father's death" (Acts 7:4). Charles 1902 notes that the Samaritan text of Genesis 11:32 gives Terah 145 years, which fits Acts. Following Singer, he thinks Jubilees wrote this scene to clear Abram of leaving his old father, a worry the rabbis also discuss (Genesis Rabbah 39). Jubilees keeps the 205 years and has Terah send Abram away in peace.

a: a tall oak
p: Like the Greek of Genesis 12:6, Jubilees has "the high oak," not "the oak of Moreh."
b: The Hebrew of Genesis 12:6 names "the great tree of Moreh" (site). The Greek Septuagint reads "the high oak" (tēn drun tēn hupsēlēn), and the Ge'ez agrees: dərsä näwaḫ, "a tall oak." Charles 1902 points this out. It is one of many places where Jubilees, in the form we have it, agrees with the Greek Bible. The Ge'ez calls Shechem Seqimon.

a: from the entrance to Hamath
p: The northern edge of the promised land, "Lebo-hamath."
b: The "entrance to Hamath" (Hebrew Lebo-hamath) is the northern border of the promised land (Numbers 34:8). Solomon's great feast drew people "from Lebo-hamath down to the Brook of Egypt" (1 Kings 8:65). Abram, standing at Shechem, sees the whole land at once, as in Genesis 13:14–15 and Deuteronomy 34:1–4.

a: To you and to your offspring I will give this land
t: The first promise of the land
p: Genesis 12:7, with "to you" added.
b: Genesis 12:7 reads "To your offspring I will give this land." Jubilees adds "to you," as Genesis itself does in Genesis 13:15 and Genesis 17:8. The promise of the land runs through the whole book, and the Plain English Translation uses "offspring" for zärʾ (seed) as the site's Genesis does.

a: He built an altar there
p: Genesis 12:7–8. Jubilees has Abram offer burnt offerings at each altar.
b: Genesis says Abram built altars and "called on the name of the LORD" (Genesis 12:7–8). Jubilees each time adds a burnt offering (13:4; 13:9; 13:16). In this book the fathers worship as Israel's priests later would, long before the tabernacle.

a: Everything grew on it
p: The list of trees recalls Moses' promise of a land of vines, figs and pomegranates.
b: Deuteronomy promises "a land of wheat and barley, of vines, figs and pomegranates" (Deuteronomy 8:8). Jubilees has Abram see such a land from the start, with water on the mountains (compare Deuteronomy 11:11). Genesis gives no description of the land at this point.

a: pines
p: The Ge'ez libanos is uncertain. Dillmann took it as "pines"; Charles changed it to "date trees."
b: VanderKam's text reads libanos. Charles 1902 reports that two of his manuscripts read the same, a word Dillmann took to mean "pine trees," while another had a garbled form that Charles corrected to bilanos, from Greek balanos, which he took as "date trees." The Plain English Translation follows the text, with Dillmann's sense. In Greek libanos is the frankincense tree.

a: on the first day of the first month
p: Abram builds an altar on the first day of the year, one of the book's four key days.
b: The first day of the first month is one of the four days that, in Jubilees, mark the seasons of its 364-day year (see 6:23). Abram honors it with an altar and a burnt offering. Charles 1902 notes that his manuscripts differ here; he preferred the reading "the first month," which VanderKam's text has. Genesis gives no dates for Abram's journeys.

a: You are my God, the eternal God
p: Later at Beersheba Abraham calls on "the Everlasting God" (Genesis 21:33).
b: In Genesis 21:33 Abraham "called on the name of the LORD, the Everlasting God" (El Olam). Jubilees gives the title to Abram's first worship in the land. Terah had used it in his blessing (12:29).

a: Hebron was built at that time
p: Jubilees builds a date out of a remark in Numbers 13:22.
b: Numbers 13:22 notes, "(Hebron had been built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.)" Jubilees turns this into history: Hebron was being built when Abram came, and Tanis (Zoan) seven years later, while Abram was in Egypt (13:12). Charles 1902 points to this source.

a: There was a famine in the land
p: Genesis 12:10.
b: "There was a famine in the land, and Abram went down to Egypt" (Genesis 12:10). In Jubilees the famine is one of Abraham's tests (17:17), as it is in rabbinic lists of his ten trials.

a: He lived in Egypt five years before his wife was taken from him
p: Jubilees drops Abram's plan to call Sarai his sister, and the rebuke Pharaoh gave him.
b: In Genesis Abram asks Sarai, "Please say you are my sister" (Genesis 12:13), and Pharaoh scolds him: "Why didn't you tell me she was your wife?" (Genesis 12:18). Jubilees says only that Sarai was taken, and Pharaoh punished. Charles 1902: the author hides Abram's deception. Differs from the Bible: Genesis tells the father's faults openly. Jubilees, wanting a blameless model for its readers, leaves them out here and again in 16:10.

a: Tanis in Egypt
p: The Ge'ez uses the Greek name Tanis for the city Hebrew calls Zoan.
b: The Ge'ez Ṭänays is the Greek name Tanis, which the Septuagint uses for Hebrew Ṣoʿan, Zoan (Charles 1902). It was a great city of the eastern Nile Delta, named in Numbers 13:22, Psalm 78:12 and Isaiah 19:11.

a: horses
p: Genesis lists sheep, cattle, donkeys, slaves and camels. Jubilees adds horses.
b: Genesis 12:16 lists "sheep and cattle, male donkeys, male and female slaves, female donkeys and camels," and Genesis 13:2 adds silver and gold. Jubilees adds horses. A small addition, but it shows the book reshaping the lists of Genesis freely.

a: He blessed the Lord his God, who had brought him back in peace
p: Genesis 13:1–4: Abram returns to the altar between Bethel and Ai.
b: Genesis says Abram went back "to the place between Bethel and Ai where his tent had stood at the beginning, the place of the altar" (Genesis 13:3–4). Jubilees adds Pharaoh's sending him away (from Genesis 12:20) and a blessing for a safe return.

a: Lot parted from him
p: Jubilees drops the strife over pasture and Lot's choice of the Jordan plain.
b: Genesis tells how the land could not hold both families, how their herders quarreled, and how Abram let Lot choose first (Genesis 13:5–12). Jubilees gives one line: Lot parted from him and settled in Sodom. It keeps the warning of Genesis 13:13, "Now the men of Sodom were evil, great sinners against the LORD" (Genesis 13:13), which prepares for chapter 16.

a: It grieved Abram to the heart
p: Jubilees adds that Abram grieved, because Lot had been like a son to the childless man.
b: Terah had told Abram to take Lot "as your own son" (12:30). Now Lot is gone and Abram has no heir. Genesis does not say how Abram felt. Charles 1902 notes that his manuscripts differ on the verb, but all give this sense. The grief sets up God's promise in the next verses.

a: In that year, when Lot was taken captive
t: A promise in a year of war
p: The book ties God's promise of the land to the year of Lot's capture (13:22-23).
b: Genesis places the promise right after Lot's departure (Genesis 13:14) and the war of the kings in the next chapter. Jubilees dates both to the same year, the fourth of the week, so that the promise of countless offspring comes in the year Abram loses Lot to an enemy.
orig: በውእቱ ዓመት አመ ተፄወወ ሎጥ (bäwʾətu ʿamät ʾämä täḍewäwä loṭ)

a: Even if someone could count the sand of the earth, your offspring could not be counted
t: Even if the sand could be counted
p: Genesis 13:16 says the opposite way round: if the dust could be counted, so could your offspring.
b: Genesis 13:16 reads: "If anyone could count the dust of the earth, then your offspring could be counted too." The Ge'ez has a negative: even if one could count the sand, your offspring could not be counted. Charles 1902 notes that the Aramaic Targum Onkelos has the negative too. The comparison with "the sand of the sea" comes from later promises (Genesis 22:17; Genesis 32:12).

a: Get up and walk its length and its width
p: Genesis 13:17-18.
b: "Get up and walk through the land, its length and its width, for I will give it to you" (Genesis 13:17). The Ge'ez lacks "through the land," which Charles 1902 added from Genesis; the Plain English Translation keeps the text. Genesis 13:18 sends Abram to "the great trees of Mamre, which are at Hebron."

a: Arioch king of Sellasar and Tergal king of the nations
p: The Ge'ez names match the Greek Bible more than the Hebrew: Sellasar, Tergal.
b: Genesis 14:1 lists "Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam and Tidal king of Goiim." The Ge'ez has Kädälägomor, ʾAmärfal, Seläsar and Tergal. Charles 1902 notes that the Greek manuscript of Genesis 14:1 he calls A has Sellasar, and he gives the Septuagint's form of Tidal as Thargal (Swete's Septuagint, printed from Codex Vaticanus, has Ellasar and Thalga). "King of the nations" translates the Hebrew name Goiim, which means "nations."
orig: ወአሪአክ ንጉሠ ሴለሳር ወቴርጋል ንጉሠ አሕዛብ (wäʾäriʾäk nəguśä seläsar wätergal nəguśä ʾäḥzab)

a: They killed the king of Gomorrah, and the king of Sodom ran away
p: In Genesis the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fall in the tar pits, yet Sodom's king meets Abram later.
b: Genesis 14:10 says the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah "fell there" in the tar pits, but the king of Sodom comes out to meet Abram in Genesis 14:17. Charles 1902 thinks Jubilees fixes the apparent clash: the king of Gomorrah is killed, the king of Sodom escapes. Many readers of Genesis take "fell" to mean they jumped or hid in the pits, which removes the problem in another way.

a: and he went off as far as Dan
p: The Ge'ez has "he," the enemy king. Charles changed it to "they."
b: VanderKam's text reads wäḥorä, "and he went," most likely Chedorlaomer with his army. Charles 1902 emended it to "they went." In Genesis 14:14 it is Abram who chases the enemy "as far as Dan." Jubilees has the captors carry Lot north to Dan, and the next verses compress Abram's pursuit into a line.

a: He armed the servants born in his house
p: Jubilees reads Genesis 14:14 as "armed," like the Aramaic Targum; the Greek has "counted."
b: The Hebrew of Genesis 14:14, wayyareq, is rare: it may mean "he drew out" or "he armed" his trained men. Charles 1902 notes that the Targum Onkelos supports "armed," while the Septuagint and the Vulgate have "he counted." The Ge'ez ʾästäräsäyä means "he armed." Jubilees leaves out the number 318.

a: gave it to Melchizedek
p: Only VanderKam's bracketed words name Melchizedek. The manuscripts Charles used have a gap here.
b: Genesis 14:17–20 tells of Melchizedek, king of Salem and "priest of God Most High," who blessed Abram and received a tenth (Genesis 14:18–20). Hebrews builds a whole argument on him (Hebrews 7:1–10). In the manuscripts Charles used, Jubilees breaks off exactly here and resumes in the middle of a sentence about the tithe (see the variant on this verse). The words that name Melchizedek stand in square brackets in VanderKam's text; the text as transcribed for this site does not show whether they come from a manuscript or are the editor's restoration. So we cannot be sure what Jubilees first said about him. The bracketed words also say more than Genesis: Abram "killed Chedorlaomer." Genesis says only that he "struck them, and chased them as far as Hobah, north of Damascus" (Genesis 14:15).

a: the first tithe, for the Lord
p: ʿAśratä qädami: "the first tithe." Jubilees later speaks of a second tithe (32:10-11).
b: The Ge'ez can mean "the first tithe" or "a tenth of the first (fruits)"; Charles 1902 chose the second. Later the book commands "a second tithe" to be eaten each year before the Lord (32:10–11). Tobit also knows more than one tithe: he gives a tenth to the Levites, and "For six years out of seven I set aside the second tenth in money, and every year I went and spent it in Jerusalem" (Tobit 1:7); in the third year he gives to orphans, widows and converts (Tobit 1:8). Jubilees, unlike Tobit, gives the first tithe to the priests, not the Levites (13:25).

a: to the priests who serve before him
p: Jubilees grounds the law of the tithe in Abram's gift. Hebrews uses the same story differently.
b: Goes beyond: in Numbers the tithe goes to the Levites, who give a tenth of it to the priests (Numbers 18:21–26). Jubilees says the Lord set it for the priests, forever, starting from Abram's tithe. Hebrews uses Abram's tithe to argue the reverse: Melchizedek, who was not of Levi, received a tithe from Abraham, so his priesthood is greater than Levi's (Hebrews 7:4–10). For how the churches answer whether Christians must tithe, see the cards at Leviticus 27 and Malachi 3.

a: There is no limit of days to this law
t: A law with no end date
p: The book's formula for a permanent law; it comes back for Booths (16:30).
b: "There is no limit of days" (ʾälbo ... wäsänä mäwaʿl) is how Jubilees says a law never expires. The same words return for the Feast of Booths (16:30), and close ones for the second tithe (32:10). The list "grain, wine and oil, cattle and sheep" follows the law of the tithe in Deuteronomy 14:23 and Leviticus 27:30–32.
orig: ወአልቦ ለዝ ሕግ ወሰነ መዋዕል (wäʾälbo läz ḥəg wäsänä mäwaʿl)

a: He gave it to his priests to eat and drink with joy before him
p: Deuteronomy has the giver eat the tithe before the Lord with joy; here the priests eat it.
b: Deuteronomy tells the giver to bring the tithe to the chosen place and "Eat there before the LORD your God and rejoice, you and your household" (Deuteronomy 14:26). Jubilees keeps the joy and the eating before God, but gives the first tithe to the priests. The giver's own feast it saves for the second tithe (32:10–11).

a: I raise my hands to God Most High
t: Abram's oath to the king of Sodom
p: Genesis 14:21–24, with the site's wording, except that Jubilees has only "God Most High."
b: Jubilees follows Genesis 14:21–24 closely. In the Hebrew of Genesis 14:22 Abram swears "to the LORD, God Most High"; the Ge'ez has only "God Most High," and "hands" in the plural. The three allies appear in Ge'ez as ʾAwnan, ʾEskal and Mamri: Aner, Eshcol and Mamre (Genesis 14:13).

a: on the first day of the third month
t: The covenant in the third month
p: Jubilees dates the covenant between the pieces to the month of the Feast of Weeks.
b: Genesis 15 gives no date. Jubilees puts God's word on the first day of the third month and the sacrifice in the middle of the month (14:10), the date the book gives for the Feast of Weeks and for God's covenant with Noah (6:17; 14:20). Charles 1902 argues that the book kept that feast on the fifteenth of the third month. In Exodus Israel reaches Sinai in the third month too (Exodus 19:1).

a: in a dream
p: Genesis 15:1 says "in a vision"; the Ge'ez says "in a dream."
b: The site's Genesis 15:1 reads "in a vision" (Hebrew maḥazeh). The Ge'ez has bäḥəlm, "in a dream." Later in the chapter Abram falls into a trance and then wakes (14:13, 14:17), so the book treats the whole scene as a night revelation.

a: I am your protector
p: Genesis 15:1 has "a shield for you"; the Ge'ez has "your protector."
b: The Hebrew magen is a shield. The Ge'ez qawm means one who stands up for another, a protector. The meaning is the same: God stands between Abram and harm. Psalm 3:3 and Psalm 84:11 use the shield image for God.

a: The son of Maseq, my slave woman, is Eliezer of Damascus
p: Hebrew ben-mesheq ("son of possession"?) became a woman named Maseq.
b: Genesis 15:2 has the puzzling Hebrew ben-mesheq beti, perhaps meaning the heir of his household (the site: "the one who will own my household"). Charles 1902 says the Greek translators took mesheq as a person's name. The Ge'ez goes one step further and makes Maseq Abram's slave woman (ʾämätyä), the mother of Eliezer. Likely mistranslation: Genesis has no woman named Maseq.
orig: ወወልደ ማሴቅ አመትየ (wäwäldä maseq ʾämätyä); Hebrew וּבֶן־מֶשֶׁק בֵּיתִי (uven-mesheq beti)

a: Abram put his trust in the Lord, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness
p: Genesis 15:6, the verse Paul and James build on. Jubilees passes over it without comment.
b: Jubilees copies Genesis 15:6 and moves on. Paul makes it the center of his case that God counts faith as righteousness "not when he was circumcised, but when he was uncircumcised" (Romans 4:10; Galatians 3:6). James joins it to the binding of Isaac (James 2:21–23). 1 Maccabees 2:52 asks, "Abraham: was he not found faithful in the test, and was it not reckoned to him as righteousness?", closer to Jubilees' own picture of Abraham tested and found faithful (17:17–18). How the churches read the verse is set out in the card at Genesis 15.
r: Genesis 15:6; Romans 4:3; Romans 4:9–11; Galatians 3:6; James 2:21–23; 1 Maccabees 2:52

a: to give you the land of the Canaanites to hold forever
p: Genesis 15:7, with "the land of the Canaanites" and "forever" added.
b: "I am the LORD, who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land to possess" (Genesis 15:7). Jubilees adds "forever" and the promise to be God to Abram's offspring (as in Genesis 17:7). Nehemiah 9:7 recalls the same act. The later legend of Abram's rescue from the fire grew partly out of this verse (see 12:12).

a: a three-year-old heifer
t: One of each, or three of each?
p: Jubilees, like the Hebrew and Greek, has one animal of each kind. Some Jewish readers counted three.
b: Charles 1902 notes that the Hebrew text, the Septuagint and Targum Pseudo-Jonathan of Genesis 15:9 give one animal of each kind, as Jubilees does. The Targum Onkelos and Genesis Rabbah read the Hebrew meshulleshet, "three-year-old," as "three" of each, and Rashi and other medieval commentators followed them (Charles, citing Beer).

a: in the middle of the month
p: The sacrifice falls on the fifteenth of the third month, the book's date for the Feast of Weeks.
b: "The middle of the month" is the fifteenth. In Jubilees this is the day of the Feast of Weeks (15:1; 16:13). Charles 1902 notes that other Jewish chronologies put the covenant between the pieces on the fifteenth of the first month, the night of Passover (Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Exodus 12:40; Seder Olam 5), linking the promise of the Exodus to the Exodus night.

a: He poured out their blood on the altar
p: In Genesis Abram cuts the animals for a covenant rite. Jubilees adds an altar and blood on it.
b: In Genesis 15 there is no altar: Abram cuts the animals in two, and God's fire passes between the pieces (Genesis 15:10, 17). Jubilees adds an altar, the pouring of blood on it (as in Leviticus 1:5), and in 14:19 the burning of the pieces as an offering. Goes beyond the Bible: the book makes Abram's rite match the later law of sacrifice.

a: Abram kept them away
p: Jubilees agrees with the Hebrew ("drove them away"); the Greek has Abram "sat with them."
b: The Hebrew of Genesis 15:11 says Abram "drove them away." The Septuagint reads kai sunekathisen autois Abram, "and Abram sat down with them" (Charles 1902). The Ge'ez agrees with the Hebrew. The birds coming down on the pieces echo the ravens of 11:11–24: once more Abram guards what is God's from birds of prey.

a: the laid-out pieces
p: The Ge'ez word means "what is spread out." Charles changed it to "pieces."
b: The Ge'ez səfḥ means "that which is spread out," and it returns in 14:17 and 14:19. Charles 1902 thought it a slip in the Greek behind the Ge'ez, for a word meaning "the cut pieces" (as the Septuagint's "the halves"), or else for "carcasses" (the Hebrew pegarim of Genesis 15:11). The Plain English Translation keeps the text: the halves laid out on the ground.

a: a trance fell on Abram
p: Hebrew "deep sleep"; the Greek and the Ge'ez have a trance.
b: Genesis 15:12 uses tardemah, the deep sleep God also sent on Adam (Genesis 2:21; the site: "a deep sleep fell on Abram"). The Septuagint renders it ekstasis, "a trance," and the Ge'ez dəngaḍe, "amazement, trance," agrees with the Greek.
orig: ድንጋፄ ወድቀ ላዕለ አብራም (dəngaḍe wädqä laʿlä ʾäbram)

a: for four hundred years
t: Four hundred or four hundred and thirty?
p: Genesis 15:13 says four hundred years; Exodus 12:40 says four hundred and thirty.
b: "The Israelites had lived in Egypt for a span of four hundred and thirty years" (Exodus 12:40), but Genesis 15:13 and Acts 7:6 say four hundred. Charles 1902 sets out the old answers: the Septuagint of Exodus 12:40 adds "and in the land of Canaan," counting the fathers' years there; Paul counts 430 years from the promise to the law (Galatians 3:17); Jubilees itself counts from Isaac's birth. Charles also notes that Jubilees, like the Septuagint and Vulgate, has "they will enslave them," where the Hebrew says "they will serve them."

a: In the fourth generation
t: A generation of a hundred years
p: Charles took "generation" here as a hundred years, Abram's age when Isaac was born.
b: If four generations match four hundred years (14:13), each is a hundred years. Charles 1902 points out that Abraham was a hundred when Isaac was born (Genesis 21:5). Genesis 15:16 has the same wording, and Exodus 6:16–20 counts four generations from Levi to Moses.

a: There was an oven, smoking, and a flame of fire passed between the laid-out pieces
p: An old way of making a covenant: the one who swears walks between the halves.
b: Jeremiah describes the rite: the leaders "cut in two and passed between its pieces" when they made a covenant, and God will treat the oath-breakers like the calf (Jeremiah 34:18). In Genesis 15:17 only God's fire passes between, so God alone takes the oath. Jubilees keeps this: Abram sleeps, and the flame passes.

a: the Phakorites, the Hivites
p: Jubilees lacks the Hittites and adds the Phakorites and the Hivites.
b: Genesis 15:19–21 lists ten peoples, among them the Hittites. The Ge'ez list has eleven: no Hittites, but "Phakorites" (fäkärews, a name found nowhere else) and the Hivites. Charles 1902 notes that the Hivites stand in the Samaritan and Greek texts of Genesis 15:20 but not in the Hebrew, Syriac or Latin.

a: Abram offered up the laid-out pieces and the birds
t: The pieces burned as an offering
p: Genesis ends with God's promise. Jubilees adds that Abram burned the pieces on the altar.
b: In Genesis the rite ends when God's fire passes between the pieces and God speaks (Genesis 15:17–21). Jubilees adds a whole sacrifice, with offerings and drink offerings. Goes beyond: for this book a covenant day is a feast day, kept with sacrifice, as Abram will keep it every year (14:20).

a: like the covenant we had made with Noah in this month
p: The covenant with Abram falls on the day of Noah's covenant, the Feast of Weeks.
b: In 6:17 the heavenly tablets order that the Feast of Weeks be kept "in this month once a year, to renew the covenant" made with Noah. Now Abram's covenant falls on the same feast, and he "renewed" it. Jubilees reads the covenants of Genesis as one covenant renewed. Christians later linked the same feast, Pentecost, with the gift of the Spirit (Acts 2:1).

a: Maybe I can build up offspring for you through her
p: Genesis 16:2. Hebrew plays on "be built" and "son."
b: "Go in to my slave woman. Maybe I can be built into a family through her" (Genesis 16:2). The Hebrew ʾibbaneh, "I will be built," sounds like ben, "son." The Ge'ez keeps the building image: ʾäḥänṣ, "I will build." Jubilees leaves out Sarai's words that "the LORD has held me back."
orig: እመቦ ከመ አሐንጽ ለከ እምኔሃ ዘርአ (ʾəmäbo kämä ʾäḥänṣ läkä ʾəmneha zärʾä)

a: He named him Ishmael
p: Jubilees skips Hagar's flight and the angel at the spring (Genesis 16:4-14).
b: Between Hagar's conceiving and Ishmael's birth, Genesis tells of Sarai's harshness, Hagar's flight, and the angel of the LORD who finds her and names the child (Genesis 16:4–14). Jubilees goes straight to the birth, as in Genesis 16:15–16: "Abram was eighty-six when Hagar bore Ishmael to him." Differs: the book leaves out a story where the household of Abram does not look good, and one where God shows special care for Ishmael's mother. The book's own dates do not agree with this age. "The fifth year of this week" is the fifth year of the first week of the forty-first jubilee (13:16), that is, 40 × 49 + 5 = year 1965 from creation (Charles 1902 gives the same year); Abram was born in 1876 (11:15), which would make him 89. The mismatch is the text's.

a: the feast of the firstfruits of the wheat harvest
t: Abram keeps the Feast of Weeks
p: The feast of the first wheat is the Feast of Weeks, kept here by Abram on the fifteenth of the third month.
b: Exodus names it: "Hold the Feast of Weeks, with the first crops of the wheat harvest" (Exodus 34:22). Jubilees has Abram keep it with new grain long before Sinai, as Noah did (6:17–18), and Isaac will be born on it (16:13). Goes beyond the Bible: Genesis has no feasts before the Exodus. On the date of the feast, and why Jews disagreed about it, see this chapter's page.
orig: በዓለ ቀዳሜ ማእረረ ዘዘርአ ሥርናይ (bäʿalä qädame maʾrärä zäzärʾä śərnay)

a: a young cow, a ram and a sheep
p: The same three animals as the covenant sacrifice (14:9), not those of Leviticus 23.
b: Charles 1902 notes that these are not the offerings the law prescribes for the Feast of Weeks (Leviticus 23:18–20: seven lambs, a young bull, two rams). They repeat the animals of the covenant between the pieces (14:9), tying this feast to that covenant. The Ge'ez word for the second animal, bäḥakʷ, is rendered "ram" here as in 16:22–23; Charles rendered it "goat" in this verse.

a: I am God Almighty
p: The Ge'ez keeps the Hebrew title: ʾAmlakä Säday, "God Shaddai."
b: Genesis 17:1 has El Shaddai, which the site renders "God Almighty." The Ge'ez does not translate it but writes ʾamlakä säday, God Shaddai. The Plain English Translation uses the site's Genesis wording.

a: Be pleasing in my sight, and be whole
p: Genesis 17:1 says "Go about your life in my sight"; the Ge'ez, like the Greek, has "be pleasing."
b: The Hebrew of Genesis 17:1 says literally "walk before me." Charles 1902 notes that the Septuagint ("be well-pleasing before me"), the Syriac and the Ge'ez all give a free sense: ʾäśmər bäqdəmeyä, "please (me) before me." Hebrews 11:5–6 uses the Greek form of the idea for Enoch, who "pleased God."
orig: ወአሥምር በቅድሜየ ወኩን ፍጹመ (wäʾäśmər bäqdəmeyä wäkun fəṣumä)

a: Here is my ordinance with you
p: Where Genesis 17:4 says "my covenant," the Ge'ez says "my ordinance."
b: Genesis 17:4 reads "my covenant is with you." The Ge'ez has śərʿatyä, "my ordinance," the book's word for a fixed rule of the heavenly tablets. For Jubilees God's covenant with Abraham is also a law to be kept, above all the law of circumcision that follows (15:11–14, 25–34).

a: From now on and forever your name will be Abraham
p: Genesis 17:5.
b: "No longer will you be called Abram. Abraham will be your name, because I have made you father of a multitude of nations" (Genesis 17:5). The Ge'ez spells the new name ʾAbrəham; from here the book uses it. Nehemiah 9:7 praises God, "who chose Abram ... and made his name Abraham."

a: It will be the sign of my ordinance forever between me and you
p: Genesis 17:9-11. Paul calls circumcision "a sign, a seal."
b: "That will be the sign of the covenant between me and you" (Genesis 17:11). Paul calls Abraham's circumcision "a sign, a seal on the righteousness that came from his faith when he was still uncircumcised" (Romans 4:11). Jubilees again says "ordinance" where Genesis says "covenant."

a: You are to circumcise the child on the eighth day
p: Genesis 17:12 says "at eight days old"; Jubilees says "on the eighth day," with no leeway.
b: Charles 1902 notes that this wording, "the child on the eighth day," is found only here and in the Ethiopic Bible's Genesis 17:12, and he thinks it deliberate. Leviticus 12:3 says, "On the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin is to be circumcised." The book insists on the exact day (15:25–26). The New Testament records it for John, Jesus and Paul (Luke 1:59; Luke 2:21; Philippians 3:5).
orig: ወለወልድ አመ ሳምንት ዕለት ትከስብዎ (wäläwäld ʾämä samnət ʿəlät təkäsbəwo)

a: was not cut on the eighth day
p: The Hebrew of Genesis 17:14 lacks "on the eighth day"; the Greek and Samaritan texts have it.
b: Charles 1902 notes that "on the eighth day" is missing from the Hebrew, Syriac and Latin of Genesis 17:14 but stands in the Samaritan text and the Septuagint (tē hēmera tē ogdoē), and in quotations by Origen and Ambrose. So Jubilees here agrees with a form of Genesis that was read in its day, not with the later standard Hebrew.

a: I will bless him, and he will become a people
p: The Hebrew of Genesis 17:16 says Sarah will become nations; here, as in the Greek, it is the son.
b: In the Hebrew of Genesis 17:16 the whole verse is about Sarah: "I will bless her, and she will become nations." Charles 1902 notes that the Samaritan, Septuagint, Syriac and Vulgate read "I will bless him" in the second half, as Jubilees does. The Septuagint reads kai eulogēsō auton.

a: Abraham fell on his face and was glad
p: In Genesis 17:17 Abraham laughs. In Jubilees he rejoices.
b: "Abraham fell on his face and laughed" (Genesis 17:17), and the laugh gives Isaac his name (Hebrew yitsḥaq, "he laughs"). Jubilees has wätäfäśḥä, "he rejoiced," removing any hint of doubt. Jesus says, "Abraham your father was overjoyed that he would see my day" (John 8:56), which some readers connect with this rejoicing. Jubilees keeps the laughter for Sarah (16:2).

a: Yes.
p: The Hebrew word ʾaval can mean "truly" or "no, rather." The Ge'ez says "yes."
b: God answers Abraham's wish for Ishmael with Hebrew ʾaval, which can mean "truly" or "no, but." The site's Genesis 17:19 reads "No, your wife Sarah will bear you a son." The Ge'ez has ʾoho, "yes," and Charles rendered "Yea." On either reading God promises Isaac and also blesses Ishmael (15:20).

a: He will father twelve chieftains
p: The Ge'ez word usually means "angels"; here it has its other sense, "rulers, chiefs."
b: Genesis 17:20 promises Ishmael "twelve chieftains" (Hebrew nesiʾim), named in Genesis 25:13–16. The Ge'ez word is mälaʾəkt, the plural of mälʾak, whose usual sense is "messenger, angel." Dillmann's Lexicon (1865, under mälʾak) gives it a third sense, "ruler, prince, chief" (Latin legatus, princeps, praefectus, dux), and cites the Ge'ez Bible using it for the leaders of Israel's tribes (Numbers 7:2) and for the men over Pharaoh's livestock (Genesis 47:6). So the Ge'ez itself can say "chiefs," and "twelve angels" would make no sense in a promise of descendants. The Plain English Translation uses the site's Genesis wording, "chieftains." Charles rendered "princes"; the Septuagint of Genesis 17:20 has "twelve nations" (dōdeka ethnē).

a: every male in his house
p: Genesis 17:23-27.
b: Jubilees follows Genesis 17:23–27 but drops the ages, Abraham 99 and Ishmael 13 (Genesis 17:24–25). By this book's insistence on the eighth day, Isaac will be "the first to be circumcised by the covenant" (16:14).

a: The days may not be cut short
p: The Ge'ez puns: there is no "circumcising" (cutting short) of the eight days.
b: The words are ʾälbo kəsbätä mäwaʿl, literally "there is no circumcision of the days," using the same word as for the rite itself. Charles 1902 kept it literally. The sense, with the next clause, is that the eight days are neither cut short nor stretched. Charles quotes the later rule of the Mishnah (Shabbat 19:5), which allowed the ninth to the twelfth day in some cases, and he notes that the Samaritans and the Beta Israel of Ethiopia kept the strict eighth day, as Jubilees does.

a: written on the heavenly tablets
p: Ṣəlatä sämay: the book's name for the heavenly record of God's laws and decrees.
b: This is the first mention of the heavenly tablets in chapters 11–16; they return in 16:3, 16:9, 16:28 and 16:29. The Plain English Translation uses the same English as for 1 Enoch's heavenly tablets, though the Ge'ez word differs (see 3:10). In Jubilees what is "written on the heavenly tablets" binds forever, whether a law, a name (16:3) or a judgment (16:9).

a: He belongs to the children of destruction
p: Jubilees: no eighth-day circumcision, no place among God's people. The New Testament disagrees.
b: For Jubilees the eighth-day cut is the mark that one "belongs to the Lord"; without it a man is "for ruin." Conflicts with the New Testament: Paul writes, "real circumcision is not the outward mark in the flesh" (Romans 2:28), and the council of Acts 15 refused to require circumcision of Gentile believers (Acts 15:1; Acts 15:5; Acts 15:19–20). Deuteronomy already speaks of circumcising the heart (Deuteronomy 10:16; Deuteronomy 30:6). On whether circumcision points to infant baptism, see the card at Genesis 17.
orig: እስመ እምነ ውሉደ ሙስና (ʾəsmä ʾəmnä wəludä musna)

a: were made this way from the day they were created
p: The two highest kinds of angels were made circumcised, and Israel is made holy with them.
b: "This way" means circumcised. Charles 1902 explains: the same two orders, the angels of the presence and the angels of holiness, keep the Sabbath with God in 2:18, and here they share the sign of circumcision. Israel is raised to their company: holy "to be with him and with his holy angels." Goes beyond the Bible: no book of the 66 says this. Jesus says the risen will be "like angels" (Mark 12:25), but in a different sense.
orig: ከመዝ ፍጥረቶሙ እምዕለተ ፍጥረቶሙ (kämäz fəṭrätomu ʾəmʿəlätä fəṭrätomu)

a: He did not choose them for being children of Abraham, because he knew them
t: Not every child of Abraham is chosen
p: Ishmael and Esau are Abraham's sons but not chosen. Paul and John the Baptist make a related point.
b: The Ge'ez is hard: it may mean God did not choose them merely because they were Abraham's sons, since he knew what they were. Charles 1902 notes that "choose in them" copies a Hebrew idiom. Agrees in idea: Paul writes, "being Abraham's offspring does not make them all his children" (Romans 9:7), and John the Baptist warns, "Don't get the idea of telling yourselves, 'Our father is Abraham'" (Matthew 3:9). Differs: Paul and John open God's family to outsiders by faith (Galatians 3:7), while Jubilees closes it to all but Jacob's line.

a: Over all of them he set spirits in power, to lead them astray from him
p: Each nation has a spirit over it, set there to lead it astray. Israel has God alone.
b: Deuteronomy 32:8 says that when the Most High divided the nations, "he marked out the peoples' borders / to match the number of the sons of God". That is the reading of the Dead Sea Scroll 4QDeut-j, which the site follows; most Septuagint manuscripts have "the angels of God," and the Masoretic Text "the sons of Israel" (see the variant at Deuteronomy 32:8). Sirach puts it this way: "For each nation he appointed a ruler, / but Israel is the Lord's share" (Sirach 17:17). Daniel speaks of the princes of Persia and Greece (Daniel 10:13; Daniel 10:20). Goes beyond: no book of the 66 says God set these spirits over the nations to mislead them. Charles 1902 suggests the book states the result as if it were the purpose, as Isaiah 6:9–10 does. Paul calls the powers that once held Gentiles "the basic elements of the world" (Galatians 4:3).
r: Deuteronomy 32:8–9; Sirach 17:17; Daniel 10:13; Daniel 10:20–21; Galatians 4:3; 1 Kings 22:19–23

a: he alone is their ruler
p: Jubilees says no angel rules Israel. Daniel names Michael as Israel's prince.
b: "For the LORD's own share is his people" (Deuteronomy 32:9). Jubilees draws from this that Israel has no angel ruler at all. Differs from Daniel: Daniel calls Michael "your prince" (Daniel 10:21; Daniel 12:1), and Charles 1902 notes that 1 Enoch puts Israel for a time under seventy angel shepherds (1 Enoch 89:59). Jubilees stresses instead that God himself guards Israel and will call the angels to account for it.

a: they will leave some of the flesh of circumcision
p: The Ge'ez says they will "leave a remainder" of the flesh. Charles took it as "omit."
b: The words are yəkäwnu mätrəfanä, "they will be ones who leave (something) remaining," in the flesh of circumcision. Read literally, the prophecy is against a cut that leaves part of the foreskin. Charles 1902 rendered it "they will omit this circumcision." Either way the next sentence goes further: some will not circumcise at all. 1 Maccabees describes Jews in the 170s BC who "made foreskins for themselves and turned away from the holy covenant" (1 Maccabees 1:15).
orig: እስመ እምሥጋ ክስበቶሙ ይከውኑ መትርፋነ (ʾəsmä ʾəmśəga kəsbätomu yəkäwnu mätrəfanä)

a: sons of Beliar
p: Belʾar: a name for the evil spirit, as in 2 Corinthians 6:15.
b: The Ge'ez wəludä belʾar recalls the Hebrew "sons of beliyyaʿal," "worthless men" (1 Samuel 2:12). Charles 1902 argues that by the second century BC Beliar was the name of an evil spirit, as here and in 1:20 and the Testament of Dan 5. Paul asks, "How can Christ be in tune with Beliar?" (2 Corinthians 6:15).

a: They have made themselves like the nations
p: The verb tenses slip from future to past: the writer is describing his own day.
b: The angel speaks of the future ("will be false," 15:33), but here the verbs turn to the past: "they have left," "they have made themselves like the nations." Charles 1902 says the author "has forgotten his role as a prophet." He saw in 15:33–34 the spread of this practice in the early second century BC, when 1 Maccabees says Jews joined themselves to the nations (1 Maccabees 1:11–15) and Antiochus IV forbade circumcision (1 Maccabees 1:48; 1 Maccabees 1:60–61).

a: For them there will be no more pardon or forgiveness
p: Leaving the covenant sign is called an error with no forgiveness, ever.
b: Goes beyond: the law gives no sacrifice for some sins, and Jesus speaks of a sin that "has no forgiveness, not ever" (Mark 3:29), but that is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, not neglect of circumcision. Hebrews 6:4–6 warns of falling away past repentance. Charles 1902 thinks the last clause of this verse is a copyist's repetition.

a: we appeared to Abraham at the oak of Mamre
p: Jubilees drops Abraham's meal for his three visitors (Genesis 18:2-8).
b: In Genesis the LORD appears as three men, and Abraham feeds them; they eat under the tree (Genesis 18:8). Jubilees says only "we appeared," the angels of the presence, and skips the meal. Charles 1902, following Singer, thinks the idea of angels eating gave offence. Tobit's angel says, "Now you see that I never ate anything; you were seeing a vision" (Tobit 12:19). Hebrews recalls the scene as showing hospitality to angels unawares (Hebrews 13:2).

a: denied that she had laughed
p: Genesis 18:12-15.
b: "So Sarah laughed inside herself" ... "But Sarah denied it" (Genesis 18:12, 15). In Jubilees the angels, not the LORD, rebuke her. The laughter stays with Sarah; Abraham's was turned into joy (15:17).

a: as it is set and written on the heavenly tablets: Isaac
p: Isaac's name was written on the heavenly tablets before he was born.
b: God names Isaac in Genesis 17:19 before his birth. Jubilees goes further: the name was already written in heaven. Jesus tells his disciples, "Be glad that your names stand written in heaven" (Luke 10:20), and Revelation speaks of names written in the book of life (Revelation 13:8).

a: she had conceived a son
p: The text says Sarah had conceived when the angels came back. Charles thought it corrupt.
b: The Ge'ez reads as if the angels returned and found Sarah already pregnant (wäyʾətini ḍänsät wäldä). Charles 1902 expected "she would conceive" and thought the slip was old, going back to the Greek, and that it caused a gloss in 16:15–16 (see the variant there). The Plain English Translation follows the text; it may simply look ahead to 16:12 and 16:16.

a: He burned them with fire and sulfur
p: Genesis 19:24-25. Jesus, Peter and Jude all use Sodom as the great warning.
b: "Then the LORD rained sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah" (Genesis 19:24). Jubilees adds Zeboiim (Deuteronomy 29:23). Jesus says, "on the day Lot went out from Sodom, it rained fire and sulfur from heaven and wiped them all out" (Luke 17:29). Jude and 2 Peter set Sodom as an example (Jude 7; 2 Peter 2:6).

a: committed sexual sin in their flesh
p: Jubilees names sexual impurity. Ezekiel names pride and neglect of the poor. Jude names both "sexual immorality" and "other flesh."
b: The Bible gives more than one picture. Genesis 19 tells of the men's demand to have sex with Lot's guests. Ezekiel says, "Here is the guilt of Sodom, your sister: pride, a full belly of food, and easy, quiet comfort ... But she did not strengthen the hand of the poor and needy" (Ezekiel 16:49). Jude says they "gave themselves to sexual immorality and went after other flesh" (Jude 7). Agrees with Jude: Jubilees puts the weight on sexual sin and impurity, and like Jude it draws a warning for its own readers (16:6).

a: on the places where people act like Sodom in its impurity
p: The judgment of Sodom becomes a law for every place that copies its sins.
b: Jubilees turns a past event into a standing rule: any place that does as Sodom did will be judged as Sodom was. The Bible uses Sodom the same way, as a pattern (Deuteronomy 29:23; Isaiah 1:9–10; 2 Peter 2:6: "setting them up as an example for those who would be ungodly later"). Charles 1902 notes that the Latin reads "as he judged" Sodom.

a: because the Lord remembered Abraham
p: Genesis 19:29. 2 Peter calls Lot righteous; Jubilees does not.
b: "He remembered Abraham. He sent Lot out from the middle of the ruin" (Genesis 19:29). In Jubilees Lot is saved only for Abraham's sake. 2 Peter says more: "Lot, though, was righteous, and God rescued him" (2 Peter 2:7). Differs: Jubilees gives Lot no such praise and turns at once to his sin (16:8).

a: the man lay with his daughter
p: Genesis says the daughters made Lot drunk and he did not know. Jubilees blames Lot with them.
b: In Genesis 19:30–38 the daughters plan it, give their father wine, and "He did not know when she lay down or when she got up" (Genesis 19:33). Jubilees says "Lot and his daughters committed a sin," calls it the worst since Adam's time, and ends: "the man lay with his daughter." Differs from Genesis: Genesis tells the story without a verdict; Jubilees judges Lot, in line with the law against sex with close kin (Leviticus 18:6).

a: leave that man no offspring on the earth on the day of judgment
p: Lot's descendants, Moab and Ammon, are doomed. The Bible gives them a land, and Ruth.
b: Lot's sons became Moab and Ammon (Genesis 19:37–38). Jubilees says the heavenly tablets doom all his offspring. Conflicts in part: Deuteronomy 23:3 does bar Moabites and Ammonites from the assembly of the LORD, and the prophets foretell their judgment (Zephaniah 2:9). But Deuteronomy also says God gave them their land "to the descendants of Lot as their own" (Deuteronomy 2:9; Deuteronomy 2:19), and Ruth the Moabite became the great-grandmother of David and stands in Jesus' family line (Ruth 4:17; Matthew 1:5).
r: Genesis 19:37–38; Deuteronomy 2:9; Deuteronomy 2:19; Deuteronomy 23:3; Ruth 4:17; Matthew 1:5; Zephaniah 2:9

a: between Kadesh and Shur
p: Jubilees leaves out Abraham's second "she is my sister" story (Genesis 20).
b: Genesis 20 tells how Abraham, in Gerar, again said of Sarah "She is my sister," and King Abimelech took her (Genesis 20:1–2). Charles 1902: all mention of it is left out. Jubilees keeps only the place, "between Kadesh and Shur." As in 13:11, the book will not show the father deceiving.

a: in the mountains of Gerar
p: The Ge'ez has "mountains"; the Latin has "territories."
b: The Ge'ez ʾädbarä geraron means "the mountains of Gerar." Charles 1902 notes that the Latin has "territories" and that the Ge'ez word could also be taken so. Rönsch suggested two similar Greek words, for "mountain" and "border," were confused.

a: the Well of the Oath
t: The Well of the Oath is Beersheba
p: Jubilees translates the name Beersheba instead of writing it.
b: Beersheba means "well of the oath" (or "well of seven"): "That is why the place was called Beersheba, because there the two of them swore an oath" (Genesis 21:31). The Ge'ez says ʿäzäqtä mäḥäla, "the well of the oath," and uses that name throughout.

a: On the feast of the firstfruits of the harvest Isaac was born
t: Isaac born on the Feast of Weeks
p: Isaac is born on the fifteenth of the third month. Jewish tradition gave other dates.
b: Sarah conceived in the middle of the sixth month and bore Isaac in the middle of the third: nine months. In this book's calendar that is the Feast of Weeks, the day of the covenant (14:10; 15:1). Charles 1902 notes other Jewish answers: the Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 10b) says Isaac was born at Passover, and Midrash Tanhuma on the first of Nisan. Both lines of tradition tie the promised son to a great feast.
orig: በበዓለ ቀዳሚ ማእረር ተወልደ ይስሐቅ (bäbäʿalä qädami maʾrär täwäldä yəsḥäq)

a: He was the first to be circumcised by the covenant
p: Ishmael was thirteen and Abraham ninety-nine; Isaac is the first circumcised on the eighth day.
b: "When his son Isaac was eight days old, Abraham circumcised him, as God had commanded him" (Genesis 21:4). Stephen tells it the same way: "And so Abraham fathered Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day" (Acts 7:8). For Jubilees this makes Isaac the first true member of the covenant, since the law of 15:25–26 counts only an eighth-day circumcision.

a: In the sixth year of the fourth week
p: Charles judged "fourth week" a slip for "third."
b: Charles 1902 marked "fourth" as corrupt here and in 15:1, and thought it should be "third": Ishmael was born in the fifth year of the first week of the forty-first jubilee (14:24; year 1965), and with "third" Isaac's birth falls in year 1980, "fifteen years later" in Charles's words. Genesis gives fourteen years: Abram was eighty-six at Ishmael's birth (Genesis 16:16) and a hundred at Isaac's (Genesis 21:5). The book's own dates and ages do not agree here (see the note on 14:24). The Plain English Translation keeps the text's "fourth," as VanderKam's text has it.
orig: ወበዓመት ሳድስ ዘሱባዔ ራብዕ (wäbäʿamät sads zäsubaʿe rabʿ)

a: he would not die until he had fathered six sons
p: Genesis 25:1-2: Keturah bore Abraham six sons.
b: "She bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah" (Genesis 25:2). Jubilees has the angels foretell these six sons. Charles 1902 points to the source and to 20:1, where Abraham gathers them.

a: through Isaac his name and offspring would be named
p: Genesis 21:12, quoted by Paul and by Hebrews.
b: "It is through Isaac that offspring will be named for you" (Genesis 21:12). Paul quotes it: "Your offspring will be named through Isaac" (Romans 9:7), and so does Hebrews 11:18. Jubilees will use the line again when Ishmael is sent away (17:6).

a: from the sons of Isaac one would become a holy offspring
p: Only one of Isaac's sons, Jacob, will be the holy line; Esau will be counted with the nations.
b: Jubilees narrows the chosen line again: of Abraham's sons only Isaac, of Isaac's sons only one. Charles 1902 notes that the rabbis argued whether circumcision bound Ishmael's and Keturah's sons, and held that Esau's descendants were not bound, because of Genesis 21:12. Paul uses the choice of Jacob over Esau to show that God's choosing does not rest on birth or works (Romans 9:10–13). For how the churches read that, see the cards at Romans 9 and Malachi 1.

a: a kingdom, a priesthood and a holy people
p: The promise of Sinai, given to Abraham's line in advance.
b: At Sinai God says, "out of all the peoples you will be my own private treasure" and "you will be for me a kingdom of priests, a holy nation" (Exodus 19:5–6). Jubilees gives these words to Abraham's descendants already, with "the share of the Most High" from Deuteronomy 32:9 (see 15:31–32). Peter applies the same words to the church: "a royal priesthood, a holy nation" (1 Peter 2:9).
orig: መንግሥተ ወክህነተ ወሕዝበ ቅዱሰ (mängəśtä wäkhənätä wäḥzəbä qədusä)

a: He held a feast of joy in this month for seven days
t: Abraham and the first Feast of Booths
p: Leviticus ties Booths to the wilderness; Jubilees roots it in Abraham's joy.
b: Leviticus gives the reason for the feast: "so that your descendants will know that I made the Israelites live in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt" (Leviticus 23:43). Goes beyond the Bible: Jubilees says Abraham kept it first, out of joy at the promised son, and that the angels blessed him for keeping it "at its time" (16:28). The joy matches Deuteronomy's command, "you will be nothing but glad" (Deuteronomy 16:15).

a: He was the first to keep the Feast of Booths on the earth
p: Bäʿalä mäṣälät, "the feast of shelters": Sukkot, kept in the seventh month.
b: The Ge'ez mäṣälät means shelters or shady huts, like Hebrew sukkot. The Plain English Translation uses "the Feast of Booths," as the site does in Leviticus 23:34 and John 7:2. "On the earth" may hint that the feast, like the Feast of Weeks, was already known in heaven (compare 6:18).

a: two bulls, two rams, seven sheep and one young goat for sin
p: Close to Numbers 29, but not the same: two bulls a day instead of thirteen and fewer.
b: Numbers 29:13 orders for the first day "thirteen young bulls from the herd, two rams, and fourteen male lambs in their first year," with one male goat as a sin offering (Numbers 29:16), the bulls dropping by one each day. Charles 1902 compares the lists: Abraham's rams and goat match; his bulls and sheep do not. The book shows the father keeping the feast in its own way before the law spelled it out.

a: seven rams, seven young goats, seven sheep and seven male goats
p: Four kinds, seven of each, as in Hezekiah's offering, though not the same animals.
b: Charles 1902 compares Hezekiah's rededication of the temple: "They brought seven of each, bulls, rams, lambs and male goats, as a sin offering for the kingdom" (2 Chronicles 29:21). Charles says the victims "correspond in kind and number," but the kinds are not all the same: Hezekiah's include bulls, where Jubilees has young goats. What matches is four kinds, seven of each. Here they are a peace offering (Ge'ez mäśwaʿtä mädḫanit, "offering of salvation"), the meal of joy shared with God.

a: frankincense, galbanum, stacte, nard, myrrh, sweet spice and costus
p: Exodus 30:34 names four spices for the incense; Jubilees names seven.
b: Exodus orders incense of "stacte, onycha and galbanum, spices mixed with pure frankincense, an equal part of each" (Exodus 30:34). Charles 1902 notes that Jubilees' first four match these, that Sirach 24:15 also names seven fragrances, and that the Talmud (Yoma, Keritot) speaks of these seven. The Latin version here speaks of "incense of composition," the phrase of Leviticus 4:7. The Ge'ez "in equal parts" echoes Exodus 30:34.
orig: አፈወ ስኂን ወቅንአተ ወማየ ልብን ወናርዶስ ወከርቤ ወሰንብልተ ወቍስጠ (ʾäfäwä səḫin wäqnəʾätä wämayä ləbn wänardos wäkärbe wäsänbəltä wäqʷsəṭä)

a: No foreigner was with him, and no one uncircumcised
p: Deuteronomy invites the foreigner to Booths. Jubilees shuts out the uncircumcised.
b: Deuteronomy says to rejoice at the feast with "the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow who live in your towns" (Deuteronomy 16:14). Conflicts in emphasis: Jubilees stresses that no foreigner and no uncircumcised man took part. The law does bar the uncircumcised from Passover (Exodus 12:48), and the foreigner of Deuteronomy may be one who had joined Israel. Zechariah foresees all nations coming to keep the Feast of Booths (Zechariah 14:16).

a: the plant of righteousness
p: A picture of Israel shared with 1 Enoch and Isaiah.
b: The same picture stands in 1 Enoch: "the plant of righteousness and truth will appear" (1 Enoch 10:16), and "chosen righteous ones will be chosen / from the eternal plant of righteousness" (1 Enoch 93:10). Isaiah calls the restored people "Oaks of Righteousness, / the LORD's planting" (Isaiah 61:3). Charles 1902 notes that Jubilees uses it again in 21:24.

a: to be like the one who made everything
p: A puzzling phrase: the holy offspring will be "like him who made all." Its meaning is unclear.
b: The Ge'ez reads kämä yəkun kämahu läzä gäbrä kʷəlo, "that it might be like him who made all." Charles translated it the same way without comment. It may mean that the holy line will be holy as its Maker is holy (Leviticus 19:2), or the text may be damaged. The Plain English Translation gives it as it stands.
orig: ከመ ይኩን ከማሁ ለዘ ገብረ ኵሎ (kämä yəkun kämahu läzä gäbrä kʷəlo)

a: the feast of the Lord
p: Leviticus calls Booths "the LORD's feast."
b: "Celebrate the LORD's feast for seven days" (Leviticus 23:39). In Jubilees Abraham himself gives the feast this name. The Ge'ez bäʿalä ʾəgziʾäbḥer is "feast of the Lord"; as everywhere in this book, ʾƎgziʾabḥer is "the Lord," not "the LORD."

a: put wreaths on their heads
p: Leviticus 23:40 names fruit, palms, leafy branches and willows. Wreaths are new.
b: Leviticus 23:40 lists "the fruit of beautiful trees, palm fronds, branches of thick-leaved trees and poplars of the valley stream." Jubilees keeps the branches and the "willows from the stream" (the Hebrew ʿarve-naḥal are willows or poplars) and adds wreaths on the head. Goes beyond: the wreaths are not in the Bible and may reflect the feast as it was kept in the writer's day.

a: Every day he went around the altar with the branches, seven times a day
p: The Mishnah tells of circling the altar at Booths, once a day and seven times on the seventh day.
b: The Mishnah (Sukkah 4:5) describes the temple custom: each day of the feast the people circled the altar once, crying to the LORD to save them in the words of Psalm 118:25, and on the seventh day they circled it seven times. There the branches are willows set around the altar. Jubilees has Abraham circle seven times every day, with palm fronds. The Bible itself does not mention circling the altar at this feast. John 7:37 is set on "its last and great day."
